messages.subject: dimension error in spatiotemporal model
messages.body_plain:
Hello, thank you for maintaining the nimble package!
I am trying to fit a spatiotemporal hierarchical model with nimble code as below:

intIV <- nimbleCode({

        ### Prior ####
        # betas
        beta0 ~ dflat()
        for (k in 1:p)
            betas[k] ~ dflat()
        # sigma
        sigma.U ~ dflat()
        sigma.v ~ dflat()
        sigma.delta ~ dflat()
        sigma.sigma ~ dflat()
        sigma.delta1it ~ dflat()
        sigma.betaU ~ dflat()
        sigma.betav ~ dflat()
        sigma.gamma ~ dflat()
        sigma.betag ~ dflat()

        # precision
        prec.U <- pow(sigma.U, -2)
        prec.v <- pow(sigma.v, -2)
        prec.delta <- pow(sigma.delta, -2)
        tau.sigma <- pow(sigma.sigma, -2)
        tau.delta1it <- pow(sigma.delta1it, -2)
        tau.U <- pow(sigma.U, -2)
        tau.betaU <- pow(sigma.betaU, -2)
        tau.v <- pow(sigma.v, -2)
        tau.betav <- pow(sigma.betav, -2)
        tau.gamma <- pow(sigma.gamma, -2)
        tau.betag <- pow(sigma.betag, -2)

        for (i in 1:N){
            U[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau.U)
            betaU[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau.betaU)
        }
        v[1:N] ~ dcar_normal(adj = tm.adj[1:L], num = tm.num[1:N], tau = tau.v)
        betav[1:N] ~ dcar_normal(adj = tm.adj[1:L], num = tm.num[1:N], tau = tau.betav)
        gamma[1] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
        betag[1] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
        for (t in 2:T){
            gamma[t] ~ dnorm(gamma[t-1], tau.gamma)
            betag[t] ~ dnorm(betag[t-1], tau.betag)
        }

        for (t in 2:T) {
            delta_1it[1:N, t-1] ~ dcar_normal(adj = tm.adj[1:L], num = tm.num[1:N], tau = tau.delta1it)
            }
        for (i in 1:N){
            for (t in 2:T){
                epsilonit[i,t] ~ dflat()
                delta_1it[i,t] <- delta_1it[i,t-1] + epsilonit[i,t]

            }
            for (t in 1:T){
                epsilon[i,t] ~ dflat()
                beta1[i,t] <- betaU[i] + betav[i] + betag[t] + delta_1it[i, t]
                y[i,t] ~ dnorm(beta0 + (beta1[i, t] * x[(N*(t-1))+i, 1]) + (betas %*% x[(N*(t-1))+i, 2:(p+1)]) + U[i] + v[i] + gamma[t] + epsilon[i,t], tau.sigma)

            }

        }

})

When I build the model, then it crashes with error Error in genVarInfo3() :
  Dimension of betas is 1, which does not match its usage in 'y[i, t] ~ dnorm(mean = beta0 + (beta1[i, t] * x[(3108 * (t - 1)) + i, 1]) + (betas %*% x[(3108 * (t - 1)) + i, 2:9]) + U[i] + v[i] + gamma[t] + epsilon[i, t], sd = lifted_d1_over_sqrt_oPtau_dot_sigma_cP, .tau = tau.sigma, lower_ = -Inf, upper_ = Inf, .var = lifted_d1_over_sqrt_oPtau_dot_sigma_cP * lifted_d1_over_sqrt_oPtau_dot_sigma_cP)'.
The dimensions of x is (3108*14, 9), y is (3108, 14), betas are (8), beta1 is (3108, 14). As far as I understood, the dimensions are compatible in the expression (betas %*% x[(3108 * (t - 1)) + i, 2:9]). Could anyone give any idea for the error?

Thank you very much.

messages.subject: Re: dimension error in spatiotemporal model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Insang,

Thanks for your question.  You've landed in some of the issues of types in nimble.  Because nimble generates C++ and C++ is statically typed, nimble requires stricter coding than R to ensure correct handling of types.  Types here refers to the number of indices.  As a result of static typing, matrix multiplication always returns a matrix, but you need a scalar.  In R, a 1x1 matrix may be dynamically treated as a scalar, but in nimble this must be done explicitly.  For example, if you need the result of A[,] %*% B[,] to be a vector, you can do (A[,] %*% B[,] ) [1:nrow, j], and for a scalar you can do (A[,] %*% B[,] )[1,1].  nimble is sometimes able to convert a vector (like betas) to a one-column or one-row matrix, although in your case I am wondering if you wanted x[(3108 * (t - 1)) + i, 2:9] %*% betas?  However, I think there is an easier solution for your need, which is the inprod (inner product) function.  Can you please try inprod(betas[1:8], x[(3108 * (t - 1)) + i, 2:9])?  This will return a scalar in nimble's type management system.  Also, in model code (but not nimbleFunctions), it is required to include square brackets on non-scalars.  That means you need "betas[]" or "betas[1:8]".  In the former usage, it must either be the case that nimble can determine the size of betas from other model code (which appears to be the case in your code) or that the size is provided in the dimensions argument to nimbleModel.

Here are some links that I hope are helpful:

If you are coming from BUGS or JAGS, you may find this conversion guide helpful (indexing brackets are one of the points covered): https://r-nimble.org/quick-guide-for-converting-from-jags-or-bugs-to-nimble

Information about required indexing formats in model code is in Chapter 5 of the nimble User Manual: https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-writing-models.html

Information on types in nimbleFunctions (much of which is relevant for model code) is in Section 11.3 of the User Manual: https://r-nimble.org/html_manual/cha-RCfunctions.html#sec:how-nimble-handles

Good luck and let us know how it goes.
-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Thank you for the prompt response!
Using inprod and adding brackets after betas solved my problem. But the other problem occurs when I try to compile and configure a model. When I try to run the code as below, it shows me an error message:
Rmodel <- nimbleModel(intIV, data = dat, constants, inits, returnDef = TRUE)
Error: Some items provided for compilation do not have types that can be compiled: Rmodel.  The types provided were: unknown. Be sure only specialized nimbleFunctions are provided, not nimbleFunction generators.

When I remove the returnDef argument, it compiles without errors. But in this case, I got a different error:
R3 <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
mcmc.init <- configureMCMC(R3)
Error in distInfo$discrete : $ operator is invalid for atomic vectors

I searched for the message in this forum and other sources, but the only thing I got was the link to the source code in GitHub. Maybe I am missing lots of fundamentals in nimble. I hope I could get any helps to deal with the problem.

Thank you again!

> > Thanks for your question.  You've landed in some of the issues of types in nimble.  Because nimble generates C++ and C++ is statically typed, nimble requires stricter coding than R to ensure correct handling of types.  Types here refers to the number of indices.  As a result of static typing, matrix multiplication always returns a matrix, but you need a scalar.  In R, a 1x1 matrix may be dynamically treated as a scalar, but in nimble this must be done explicitly.  For example, if you need the result of A[,] %*% B[,] to be a vector, you can do (A[,] %*% B[,] ) [1:nrow, j], and for a scalar you can do (A[,] %*% B[,] )[1,1].  nimble is sometimes able to convert a vector (like betas) to a one-column or one-row matrix, although in your case I am wondering if you wanted x[(3108 * (t - 1)) + i, 2:9] %*% betas? messages.subject: Re: dimension error in spatiotemporal model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Insang,

The problem appears to be that you declare elements of delta_1it twice, first as vector nodes following a CAR distribution and next as scalar nodes in an autoregressive structure.  This won't work.  Nodes should be declared only once.  This case got past error-trapping for duplicate declarations, so that's something we'll look at improving.

I'll offer a few additional comments that might be helpful:

You can use calculate = FALSE in nimbleModel to save time, of course without the benefit of initialized calculations, but MCMC will initialize calculations later anyway (in compiled code).

We typically pass the uncompiled model (rather than the compiled model) to configureMCMC, but either should be ok.

nimbleMCMC will call nimbleModel and compileNimble for you.  You might realize that and were breaking down the steps in a debugging effort.  One advantage of going through the handful of steps yourself is to gain control such as using calculate=FALSE in nimbleModel.

I hope you are able to get up and running now.

-Perry

messages.subject: Initializing each EnKF ensemble member
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am exploring the use of Nimble in iterative ecological forecasting.  The EnKF is particularly exciting in the nimbleSMC package. In the examples provided, the initial conditions for the latent states are defined as distributions within the nimble code and the number of ensemble members is set at the run step (Cmy_enKF$run(m = 1000)).  Is it possible to pass the initial value for each ensemble member (i.e., the last step of a previous run of the EnKF is the initial conditions for a new run of the EnKF).  This would allow an iterative approach to running the EnKF.

Here is the code I am running with the initial conditions defined within the nimble code

library("nimbleSMC")
## For illustration only.
exampleCode <- nimbleCode({
  x0 ~ dnorm(0, var = 1)
  x[1] ~ dnorm(a * x0, var = 1)
  y[1] ~ dnorm(x[1], var = .5)
  for(t in 2:10){
    x[t] ~ dnorm(a * x[t-1], var = 1)
    y[t] ~ dnorm(x[t], var = .01)
    }
  })

y <- rnorm(10)

model <- nimbleModel(code = exampleCode, data = list(y = y) , inits = list(x0 = 0, x = rnorm(10)))

model$a <- 0.8
my_enKF <- buildEnsembleKF(model, 'x',
                           control = list(saveAll = TRUE, thresh = 1))
## Now compile and run, e.g.,
Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
Cmy_enKF <- compileNimble(my_enKF, project = model)
Cmy_enKF$run(m = 1000)
enKF_X <- as.matrix(Cmy_enKF$mvSamples, 'x')

plot(enKF_X[1, ], type = "l")
for(i in 2:100){
  points(enKF_X[i, ], type = "l")
}
points(y, col = "red")

Thanks for any insight from the group!

messages.subject: Re: Initializing each EnKF ensemble member
messages.body_plain:
Hi Quinn,

Thanks for making this request.  It's great to see interest in the sequential Monte Carlo methods.

I made a rough draft for how to do this on a branch on nimble-dev/nimbleSMC on GitHub.  It took only a few small tweaks.  The methods are all written as nimbleFunctions, so you can inspect the changes without too much trouble in the source code.  Below is code to install from the branch and an expansion of the example to see (I think) that it works.  Can you give it a try and see if it does what you were looking for?

Are there any easy suggestions on how people will want to use a feature like this beyond what I drafted (one can set the first samples and then tell the EnKF to use them)?

I have a question for anyone on this list about typical use cases for Ensemble KF.   Of all the SMC methods we implemented (which are described here: https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.06206), among the developers involved we have least experience with EnKF.  Other SMC methods return both an approximate log likelihood and the filtered state samples.  The papers we worked from on EnKF emphasized state estimation, and that's what we implemented.  In practice do people make use of an approximate log likelihood from EnKF?

-Perry

library(devtools)
install_github(repo = "nimble-dev/nimbleSMC", ref = "support-recursive-use", subdir = "packages/nimbleSMC")

library("nimbleSMC")
## For illustration only.
exampleCode <- nimbleCode({
  x0 ~ dnorm(0, var = 1)
  x[1] ~ dnorm(a * x0, var = 1)

  y[1] ~ dnorm(x[1], var = .2)
  for(t in 2:10){
    x[t] ~ dnorm(a * x[t-1], sd = .2). # I changed these sds to create a more obvious visual check below
    y[t] ~ dnorm(x[t], sd = .2)
    }
  })

set.seed(3)

y <- rnorm(10)

model <- nimbleModel(code = exampleCode, data = list(y = y) , inits = list(x0 = 0, x = rnorm(10)))

model$a <- 0.8
my_enKF <- buildEnsembleKF(model, 'x',
                           control = list(saveAll = TRUE, thresh = 1))
## Now compile and run, e.g.,
Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
Cmy_enKF <- compileNimble(my_enKF, project = model)
Cmy_enKF$run(m = 1000)
enKF_X <- as.matrix(Cmy_enKF$mvSamples, 'x')

plot(enKF_X[1, ], type = "l", ylim = c(-2, 2))

for(i in 2:100){
  points(enKF_X[i, ], type = "l")
}
points(y, col = "red")

lastSamples <- enKF_X[, 'x[10]', drop=FALSE] # pull out last samples as a matrix
Cmy_enKF$setFirstSample(lastSamples)        # set them as the first samples
Cmy_enKF$run(m = 1000, skipFirst = 1)          # run again, skipping t = 1
enKF_X2 <- as.matrix(Cmy_enKF$mvSamples, 'x')
for(i in 1:100){
  points(enKF_X2[i, ], type = "l", col = 'cyan')
}

messages.body_plain:
Hi Quinn,

Great that it works for you.  Aha, thanks for explaining that about EnKF.

You are right about the values of m.  It would not make sense to use a different value in run than the size that was used in setFirstSample.  Both methods resize the modelValues object internally, so I think the practical effect will be that if m in run is larger than in setFirstSample, there will be some nonsense values used, and if it is smaller, simply not all of the "lastSamples" will be used.  But you said it broke the run, so I'll check on that later.

Unfortunately we have very limited default-value behavior supported for compiled nimbleFunctions.  We could have a default for m that is -1, which if provided means that an internal default should be used, and that internal default could be updated by setFirstSample.  The default internal default could be 100, the current default for m.  Does that makes sense?

-Perry

> One question about your update:  what happens if the ensemble size of Cmy_enKF$setFirstSample(lastSamples) differs from m in Cmy_enKF$run(m = 1000, skipFirst = 1)?  It seems like it forces m to equal  Cmy_enKF$setFirstSample(lastSamples), which seems to me to be the correct behavior.   In the example, I was confused a bit because m was included in the argument but doesn't seem necessary (it did break the run if excluded).
>

> Quinn

> >

> > > > >
> > > > > Here is the code I am running with the initial conditions defined within the nimble code
> > > > >
> > > > > library("nimbleSMC")
> > > > > ## For illustration only.
> > > > > exampleCode <- nimbleCode({
> > > > >   x0 ~ dnorm(0, var = 1)
> > > > >   x[1] ~ dnorm(a * x0, var = 1)
> > > > >   y[1] ~ dnorm(x[1], var = .5)
> > > > >   for(t in 2:10){

> > > > >     y[t] ~ dnorm(x[t], var = .01)
> > > > >     }

messages.subject: Re: Initializing each EnKF ensemble member
messages.body_plain:
Another thing to consider that would be very powerful for the ecological forecasting applications.  In your current implementation, the state variable x is initialized at x[1], the "forecast step" is applied to transition to x[2], and then the analysis step is applied the "forecasted" x[2].  So the first step is a "forecast step".  This assumes that either x[1] is initialized following an analysis step at the end of the previous run (or a forecast step if no data was available at the last step).  In an ecological forecasting application there may not have been data at the last step of the previous run (because it is a forecast of the future) but data is now available at reinitialization (because it is reinitialized one actual data later).  This means that one would want to initialize and then perform an analysis using data at t =1.  Is this feasible to implement?  (in case you are wonder who might use these features - I am leading an NSF-funded Research Coordination Network focused on ecological forecasting using NEON data.  We are actively looking for (and developing if necessary) tools for near-term iterative forecasting, especially Bayesian tools (see ecoforecast.org <http://ecoforecast.org>)

Thanks!

Quinn

messages.body_plain:
Hi Quinn,

Thanks for thinking more about this.  Let me say in more detail what I believe happens now and see if that helps sketch out improvements.

With skipFirst = FALSE (i.e. the first run), the state variable at x[1] is initialized from its prior (if you want to look at it that way) as if that is its forecast.  If there is data that depends on x[1], the filter calculations are done to create the sample of x[1] given data.  I think this is what you are calling the "analysis step" and what you were saying does not happen for x[1], by which I think you are talking about the drafted skipFirst = TRUE case (see below) but wasn't totally sure.  (Note that there can be arbitrary data that depend on each x[t], and they need not be the same in structure or distribution for each t).  If one does not want filtering at the first step or the last step as a matter of model structure, one can simply have no data nodes that depend on the state variable at one or both of those times.

Here is how I implemented your suggestion for recursive operation.   I assumed the final sample from the first EnKF run gets filtered by any observations.  That is then set as the first sample for the second EnKF run.  Separately, the skipFirst argument for the second run allows both sampling from the prior and filtering on the data to be skipped for x[1].  Hence, my assumption was that filtering happens at the end of one run and is not desired at the beginning of the next run.

I think one could achieve what you're suggesting now either by careful choice of model or by adding some switches to the algorithm.  On the model side, if you simply have a final time step with no data, you'll end up with unfiltered projections at the last time step of states.  At the first time step, one trick would be to have state "dynamics" from x[1] to x[2] that are essentially deterministic, like x[2] ~ dnorm(x[1], sd = 1e-6).  Then one could use the system I set up yesterday and make the observations at x[2] be the "new data" that really correspond to the final (unfiltered) time-step from the first EnKF run.  The alternative of adding some switches could be to provide control over whether filtering is done at the first and/or last time-steps, so that even if there are relevant data nodes, the filtering can be skipped.  This may have advantages of greater clarity (arguably) and greater flexibility to make the most of a single model and algorithm once they have been compiled (because it could be used in multiple ways rather than having the algorithm intention baked into the model structure).  At least, I think those ideas would work, but I haven't tried them!

Let me know if that all makes sense and what you think would be useful.  We could also take this off-list to go granular and then come back and share what we come up with.

-Perry

On Thu, Dec 3, 2020 at 5:36 PM Quinn Thomas <rqth...@vt.edu> wrote:

> Another thing to consider that would be very powerful for the ecological forecasting applications.  In your current implementation, the state variable x is initialized at x[1], the "forecast step" is applied to transition to x[2], and then the analysis step is applied the "forecasted" x[2].  So the first step is a "forecast step".  This assumes that either x[1] is initialized following an analysis step at the end of the previous run (or a forecast step if no data was available at the last step).  In an ecological forecasting application there may not have been data at the last step of the previous run (because it is a forecast of the future) but data is now available at reinitialization (because it is reinitialized one actual data later).  This means that one would want to initialize and then perform an analysis using data at t =1.  Is this feasible to implement?  (in case you are wonder who might use these features - I am leading an NSF-funded Research Coordination Network focused on ecological forecasting using NEON data.  We are actively looking for (and developing if necessary) tools for near-term iterative forecasting, especially Bayesian tools (see ecoforecast.org <http://ecoforecast.org>)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Insang,

There are various reasons memory use can explode for models like this.  Let me refer you to two previous threads for some of the ideas on how you can manage this: https://groups.google.com/u/2/g/nimble-users/c/8vaTHQoJz2M, https://groups.google.com/u/2/g/nimble-users/c/920URfnFiTY.

It is also important to realize that you are monitoring (in the example code you sent previously) about 87000 nodes.  That will take about 2/3 Mb per stored iteration, or about 3.25 Gb per 5000 iterations, per chain (the number that was in your example code).  That doesn't account for all the memory use, but it's worth noting.

The NA or NaN messages are saying that the log probability calculation for a node is not valid.  That usually means not that the input data for the node is invalid but that some initial values for its parent nodes are giving an invalid probability.  This may or may not be a problem. The MCMC does try to initialize everything.  A good way to diagnose issues is to run the MCMC for 0 iterations (which will trigger the initialization) and then inspect the compiled model object.  For example, if it is called Cmodel, you can do:

Cmodel$calculate("y[5, 10]") # perhaps this is NA
# Then inspect parent nodes to see how this is happening:
Cmodel$beta1[5, 10] # etc.

I hope that helps.
-Perry

messages.subject: Re: R to nimble function
messages.body_plain:
Hi Meaghan

Welcome to the wonderful world of nimble!!

One of the great things about nimble is that it gives you the flexibility to write nimble functions that can sit inside your BUGS code. So in your case you can create your own ifelse function and avoid cluttering your BUGS code as a hack.

Below is an example of how you might write your own ifelse function. In your code, just replace ifelse with myIfElse and your original code should be fine.

I normally have a script called nimbleFunctions.R to store all my nimble functions, and my main script will include the line  source("nimbleFunctions.R") early on so that I can use them. This avoids cluttering my analysis with function definitions.

Cheers
David

library(nimble)

myIfElse <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(condition = integer(0), valueIf=double(0), valueElse=double(0)) {
    returnType(double(0))
    if (condition==TRUE) {
      return(valueIf)
    } else {
      return(valueElse)
    }
  }
)

## The following is just a test to verify that the function compiles and gives sensible output.
## So use myIfElse in your BUGS code, not cIfElse.
cIfElse <- compileNimble(myIfElse)
a = 2
b = 2
cIfElse(a==b, 123, 456)
cIfElse(a==2*b, 123, 456)

messages.subject: unexpected output from compiled nimbleFunction
messages.body_plain:
Hello nimble users and developers,

Thanks very much for all your hard work building and maintaining nimble. I recently ran into some issues trying to use the "RW_llFunction_block" sampler, and I think I tracked the issue back to something having to do with the way my nimbleFunction for the log-likelihood is written to C++ and compiled. When I run the following minimal example, the compiled and uncompiled versions of llFun$run() give different answers. The compiled version is not what I'd expect to get.

library(nimble)
code <- nimbleCode({
  A[1:2, 1:2] <- diag(2) * 2
})
Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code)
llFun <- nimbleFunction(
  setup = function(model) { },
  run = function() {
    A <- model$A
    A_inv <- nimArray(0, c(2, 2, 2))
    A_inv[1, 1:2, 1:2] <- inverse(A[1:2, 1:2])
    returnType(double(2))
    return(A_inv[1, 1:2, 1:2])
  }
)
RllFun <- llFun(Rmodel)
RllFun$run()
CRll <- compileNimble(RllFun, Rmodel)
CRll$RllFun$run()

I noticed that if I change the order of the indices and replace A_inv[1, 1:2, 1:2] with A_inv[1:2, 1:2, 1] in both places it occurs, then I seem to get the right output.

Can you help me see what I'm missing?

Thanks very much for your help,
Henry Scharf

messages.subject: Re: unexpected output from compiled nimbleFunction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Henry,

Thanks for narrowing this down to a simple reproducible case.  This is a bug.   I think it has to do specifically with Eigen (C++ library) placing the solution to a matrix inverse into a map (a matrix not in contiguous memory due to indexing).  I note that for operations other than inverse, the code works, e.g if solve(A[1:2, 1:2]) is replaced with 2*A[1:2, 1:2].

Here is a workaround:

llFun <- nimbleFunction(
  setup = function(model) { },
  run = function() {
    A <- model$A
    A_inv <- nimArray(0, c(2, 2, 2))

    B <- inverse(A[1:2, 1:2])
    A_inv[1, 1:2, 1:2] <- B

    returnType(double(2))
    return(A_inv[1, 1:2, 1:2])
  }
)

(I'm not sure if you will really use larger objects, so just mentioning that for larger objects, using init=FALSE in nimArray, if you don't need the zeros as initial values, can be somewhat faster.)

-Perry

messages.subject: Re: dCRP active cluster groups
messages.body_plain:
Hi Paul,

Sorry for the late response about this and I am also sorry that I'll not give you good news.

NIMBLE’s mcmc does not handle sampling when one or more nodes in the model are functions of a node having the CRP distribution (dCRP). In your case, the functions would compute "ni" and "yi" in your previous model. So, if you need to get the unique labels and counts for the likelihood, you would not be able to sample the model.

There are still many things that we should do to use NIMBLE in more general BNP models.
Let me know if there is something else I could help with.

Best,
Claudia

messages.subject: Re: dCRP active cluster groups
messages.body_plain:
Paul, just one quick additional point.  Another possible approach to calculating the ni and yi derived quantities could be writing a separate MCMC sampler or two, serving only to calculate these quantities during the course of MCMC sampling.  This would be done independently of the updating of the CRP group-membership variables (z, in your model), and the rest of your model, and perhaps would avoid the other problems you're running into.

But, that said, I'm not entirely sure what you've implemented in C++, or how much of NIMBLE's base MCMC infrastructure you're making use of, so I'm not sure how applicable this suggestion is.  But, if some of my guesses are right, then it might easily sidestep your problem.  Happy to follow up more, if that's helpful.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Proper handling of "non-data nodes" in runCrossValidate( )
messages.subject_clean: Proper handling of "non-data nodes" in runCrossValidate( )
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

runCrossValidate( ) is throwing me an error that I suspect results from missing data in the dependent variable of a dynamic multi-species occupancy model. In the dataset, only 5 of 6 possible replicate survey visits were conducted by technicians during the first season of data collection, whereas the second season contains data for all 6 replicate visits. Therefore, the missing 6th replicate contains NAs for all sites and species in the first season. The dependent variable, called Yc, is indexed by site, species, season, and replicate, respectively.

Specifically, runCrossValidate( ) is throwing this error:
Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) :
  foldFunction is returning names of non-data nodes for fold 1
Calls: runCrossValidate -> lapply -> FUN

Here is my setup code for runCrossValidate( ), and the foldFunction is perhaps of greatest interest:
##Cross-validate model results
commNmix_FoldFunction <- function(i){
  foldNodes_i <- paste0('Yc[', i,', , , ]')  # will return 'Yc[1,,,]' for i = 1 (e.g., based on nsite)
  return(foldNodes_i)
}

##Define the loss function
#The function below computes the root mean squared error
RMSE_lossFunction <- function(simulatedDataValues, actualDataValues){
  dataLength <- length(simulatedDataValues) # simulatedDataValues is a vector
  SSE <- 0
  for(i in 1:dataLength){
    SSE <- SSE + (simulatedDataValues[i] - actualDataValues[i])^2
  }
  MSE <- SSE / dataLength
  RMSE <- sqrt(MSE)
  return(RMSE)
}

###

To use runCrossValidate( ), I simply follow the example provided in the NIMBLE package's user manual in R (see https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/nimble/versions/0.10.0/topics/runCrossValidate).

What might the "non-data nodes" error be referring to, and how can it possibly be fixed or worked around?

Best,
Andrew

messages.subject: Re: Proper handling of "non-data nodes" in runCrossValidate( )
messages.subject_clean: Proper handling of "non-data nodes" in runCrossValidate( )
messages.body_plain:
hi Andrew,

We don't consider missing observations to be data nodes (because they don't contribute to the likelihood and in an MCMC are treated as 'parameters' in the sense that they are sampled during the MCMC).
Furthermore, we can't use those nodes for cross-validation because the values are unknown. So you'd need to have your fold function avoid specifying any nodes that are missing data nodes as part of the fold.

-Chris

On Tue, Dec 8, 2020 at 11:15 AM Andrew <ajden...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello,
>
> runCrossValidate( ) is throwing me an error that I suspect results from missing data in the dependent variable of a dynamic multi-species occupancy model. In the dataset, only 5 of 6 possible replicate survey visits were conducted by technicians during the first season of data collection, whereas the second season contains data for all 6 replicate visits. Therefore, the missing 6th replicate contains NAs for all sites and species in the first season. The dependent variable, called Yc, is indexed by site, species, season, and replicate, respectively.
>
> Specifically, runCrossValidate( ) is throwing this error:
> Error in FUN(X[[i]], ...) :
>   foldFunction is returning names of non-data nodes for fold 1
> Calls: runCrossValidate -> lapply -> FUN
>
> Here is my setup code for runCrossValidate( ), and the foldFunction is perhaps of greatest interest:
> ##Cross-validate model results
> commNmix_FoldFunction <- function(i){
>   foldNodes_i <- paste0('Yc[', i,', , , ]')  # will return 'Yc[1,,,]' for i = 1 (e.g., based on nsite)
>   return(foldNodes_i)
> }
>
> ##Define the loss function
> #The function below computes the root mean squared error
> RMSE_lossFunction <- function(simulatedDataValues, actualDataValues){
>   dataLength <- length(simulatedDataValues) # simulatedDataValues is a vector
>   SSE <- 0
>   for(i in 1:dataLength){
>     SSE <- SSE + (simulatedDataValues[i] - actualDataValues[i])^2
>   }
>   MSE <- SSE / dataLength
>   RMSE <- sqrt(MSE)
>   return(RMSE)
> }
>
> ###
>
> To use runCrossValidate( ), I simply follow the example provided in the NIMBLE package's user manual in R (see https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/nimble/versions/0.10.0/topics/runCrossValidate).
>
> What might the "non-data nodes" error be referring to, and how can it possibly be fixed or worked around?
>
> Best,
> Andrew
>
>

The NA records are stored in the dependent variable at Yc[1:14, 1:26, 1, 6], for 1-14 sites, 1-26 species, season 1, and the missing 6th replicate.

How could I adapt my foldFunction to accommodate skipping over such records? Could if/then loops be used somehow?

commNmix_FoldFunction <- function(i){
  foldNodes_i <- paste0('Yc[',  i,'  ,   ,   , ]')  # will return 'Yc[1,  ,  , ]' for i = 1 (e.g., based on nsite)

messages.subject: Improving model run time - MLE/MAP initialisation
messages.subject_clean: Improving model run time - MLE/MAP initialisation
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I am currently trying to improve the run time of a model in nimble. I was thinking of reducing the burn in required by informing the initial values of the parameters using MLE or MAP estimations. Is there a way of doing this within nimble?
Any other ideas about improving the run time would also be greatly appreciated.

The model in question is for correcting delayed reporting in COVID-19 hospital deaths in England. The code is below, y[t,s] is the total number of deaths at time t in region s, and z[t,s,d] is a partial count of the deaths at time t in region s that were reported at delay d after t.

Thank you,
Alba

# Set up the splines using jagam.
blank_data=data_frame(y=rnorm(N,0,1),t=1:N,w=(1:N)%%7)
blank_jagam=jagam(y~s(t,bs='cs',k=n_knots[1])+s(w,bs='cc',k=n_knots[2]),data=blank_data,file='blank.jags',
                  knots=list(t=seq(1,C,length=n_knots[1]),w=seq(0,7,length=n_knots[2])))

# Register the Beta-Binomial as a distribution for NIMBLE (see Functions.R for dbetabin).
registerDistributions(list(dbetabin=list(
  BUGSdist='dbetabin(mu,phi,size)',discrete=TRUE)))

# NIMBLE model code.
covid_code <- nimbleCode({
  for(s in 1:S){
    for(t in 1:N){
      # Mean total deaths.
      log(lambda[t,s]) <-  iota[s] + delta[t,s]
      for(d in 1:D){
        # Expected cumulative proportions.
        probit(p[t,s,d]) <- beta[s,d] + gamma[t,s] + xi[t,s]
      }
      # Relative proportions (Beta-Binomial means).
      nu[t,s,1] <- p[t,s,1]
      for(d in 2:D){
        nu[t,s,d] <- (p[t,s,d]-p[t,s,d-1])/(1-p[t,s,d-1])
      }
    }
    for(t in 1:C){
      # Model for total deaths.
      y[t,s] ~ dnegbin(theta[s]/(theta[s]+lambda[t,s]),theta[s])
      # Model for partial reports.
      z[t,s,1] ~ dbetabin(nu[t,s,1],phi[s,1],y[t,s])
      for(d in 2:D){
        z[t,s,d] ~ dbetabin(nu[t,s,d],phi[s,d],y[t,s]-sum(z[t,s,1:(d-1)]))
      }
    }
  }
  ## Overall effects
  # Temporal spline
  Omega_alpha[1:K_t,1:K_t] <- S_t[1:K_t,1:K_t]*tau_alpha
  kappa_alpha[1:K_t] ~ dmnorm(zeros[1:K_t],Omega_alpha[1:K_t,1:K_t])
  alpha[1:N] <- X_t[1:N,1:K_t]%*%kappa_alpha[1:K_t]
  # Delay spline
  Omega_psi[1:K_t,1:K_t] <- S_t[1:K_t,1:K_t]*tau_psi
  kappa_psi[1:K_t] ~ dmnorm(zeros[1:K_t],Omega_psi[1:K_t,1:K_t])
  psi[1:N] <- X_t[1:N,1:K_t]%*%kappa_psi[1:K_t]
  # Time of week spline
  Omega_eta[1:K_w,1:K_w] <- S_w[1:K_w,1:K_w]*tau_eta
  kappa_eta[1:K_w] ~ dmnorm(zeros[1:K_w],Omega_eta[1:K_w,1:K_w])
  eta[1:N] <- X_w[1:N,1:K_w]%*%kappa_eta[1:K_w]
  ## Regional effects
  for(s in 1:S){
    Omega_delta[1:K_t,1:K_t,s] <- S_t[1:K_t,1:K_t]*tau_delta[s]
    kappa_delta[1:K_t,s] ~ dmnorm(kappa_alpha[1:K_t],Omega_delta[1:K_t,1:K_t,s])
    delta[1:N,s] <- X_t[1:N,1:K_t]%*%kappa_delta[1:K_t,s]
    # Delay spline
    Omega_gamma[1:K_t,1:K_t,s] <- S_t[1:K_t,1:K_t]*tau_gamma[s]
    kappa_gamma[1:K_t,s] ~ dmnorm(kappa_psi[1:K_t],Omega_gamma[1:K_t,1:K_t,s])
    gamma[1:N,s] <- X_t[1:N,1:K_t]%*%kappa_gamma[1:K_t,s]
    # Time of week spline
    Omega_xi[1:K_w,1:K_w,s] <- S_w[1:K_w,1:K_w]*tau_xi[s]
    kappa_xi[1:K_w,s] ~ dmnorm(kappa_eta[1:K_w],Omega_xi[1:K_w,1:K_w,s])
    xi[1:N,s] <- X_w[1:N,1:K_w]%*%kappa_xi[1:K_w,s]
  }
  # Smoothing parameter priors.
  tau_alpha ~ dinvgamma(0.5,0.5) # Equivalent to Half-Normal(0,1) on 1/sqrt(tau).
  tau_psi ~ dinvgamma(0.5,0.5)
  tau_eta ~ dinvgamma(0.5,0.5)
  for(s in 1:S){
    tau_delta[s] ~ dinvgamma(0.5,0.5)
    tau_gamma[s] ~ dinvgamma(0.5,0.5)
    tau_xi[s] ~ dinvgamma(0.5,0.5)
    for(d in 1:D){
      phi[s,d] ~ dgamma(2,0.02) # Beta-Binomial dispersion parameters.
    }
    beta[s,1] ~ dnorm(0,sd=10) # Independent delay effects.
    for(d in 2:D){
      beta[s,d] ~ T(dnorm(beta[s,d-1],sd=10),beta[s,d-1],)
    }
    iota[s] ~ dnorm(0,sd=10) # Spatial intercept.
    theta[s] ~ dgamma(2,0.02) # Negative-Binomial dispersion parameters.
  }
})

# Constants (e.g. number of days to model, number of knots) for NIMBLE.
covid_constants <- list(N=N,C=C,S=S,D=D,K_t=n_knots[1]-1,K_w=n_knots[2]-2)
# Data (e.g. total deaths, partial counts, spline model matrix) for NIMBLE.
covid_data <- list(z=z[1:C,,1:D],y=y[1:C,],X_t=blank_jagam$jags.data$X[,2:(n_knots[1])],
                   X_w=blank_jagam$jags.data$X[,(n_knots[1]+1):(n_knots[1]+n_knots[2]-2)],
                   S_t=blank_jagam$jags.data$S1,S_w=blank_jagam$jags.data$S2,
                  zeros=rep(0,max(covid_constants$K_t,covid_constants$K_w)))

# Set up the NIMBLE model for each chain.
covid_inits <- covid_model <- covid_compiled_model <- covid_mcmc_config <- covid_mcmc <- covid_compiled_mcmc <- list()
for(i in 1:n_chains){
  # Generate random initial values.
  covid_inits[[i]] <- list(kappa_alpha=rnorm(covid_constants$K_t,0,0.1),
                          kappa_psi=rnorm(covid_constants$K_t,0,0.1),kappa_eta=rnorm(covid_constants$K_w,0,0.1),
                          kappa_delta=matrix(rnorm(S*covid_constants$K_t,0,0.1),ncol=S),
                          kappa_gamma=matrix(rnorm(S*covid_constants$K_t,0,0.1),ncol=S),
                          kappa_xi=matrix(rnorm(S*covid_constants$K_w,0,0.1),ncol=S),
                          iota=rnorm(S,0,1),theta=rexp(S,0.01),tau_gamma=rinvgamma(S,0.5,0.5),
                          tau_delta=rinvgamma(S,0.5,0.5),tau_xi=rinvgamma(S,0.5,0.5),
                          phi=matrix(rexp(D*S,0.01),nrow=S,ncol=D),tau_psi=rinvgamma(1,0.5,0.5),
                          tau_alpha=rinvgamma(1,0.5,0.5),tau_eta=rinvgamma(1,0.5,0.5),
                          beta=t(apply(matrix(rnorm(D*S,0,0.1),nrow=S,ncol=D),1,sort)),y=matrix(NA,nrow=C,ncol=S),
                          z=array(NA,dim=c(C,S,D)))
  for(s in 1:S){
    for(t in 1:C){
      for(d in 1:D){
        if(is.na <http://is.na>(covid_data$z[t,s,d])) covid_inits[[i]]$z[t,s,d]=rpois(1,median(covid_data$z[,s,d],na.rm=T))
      }
      if(is.na <http://is.na>(covid_data$y[t,s])) covid_inits[[i]]$y[t,s]=sum(c(covid_inits[[i]]$z[t,s,],covid_data$z[t,s,],rpois(1,median(covid_data$y[,s]-rowSums(covid_data$z[,s,]),na.rm=T))),na.rm=TRUE)
    }
  }
  # Build the model.
  covid_model[[i]] <- nimbleModel(covid_code,covid_constants,covid_data,covid_inits[[i]])
  # Compile the model.
  covid_compiled_model[[i]] <- compileNimble(covid_model[[i]])
  # Set up the MCMC.
  covid_mcmc_config[[i]] <- configureMCMC(covid_model[[i]],monitors=c('alpha','iota','beta','psi','xi','eta',
                                                                    'theta','phi','gamma','delta','y','lambda'))
  covid_mcmc[[i]] <- buildMCMC(covid_mcmc_config[[i]])
  # Compile the MCMC.
  covid_compiled_mcmc[[i]] <- compileNimble(covid_mcmc[[i]],project=covid_model[[i]])
}

# Run the model in parallel. Change 'dopar' to 'do' to run the model on only one core.
registerDoParallel(cores=n_chains)
system.time({
  covid_samples <- as.mcmc.list(foreach(i=1:n_chains)%dopar%{
    runMCMC(covid_compiled_mcmc[[i]],niter=200000,nburnin=100000,inits=covid_inits[[i]],nchains=1,samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE,thin=10)
  })
})

Hello,

messages.body_plain:
Hi Alba,

In general using MLE or MAP as starting values is a good idea. You can do maximization directly on the likelihood or posterior density from a nimble model. Basically you need to create an R function that wraps a nimbleFunction that calculates the density of interest using model$calculate. There's a basic example here: https://github.com/nimble-dev/nimble-outreach/blob/master/modules/nimbleFunction_likCalc.Rmd

-Chris

messages.body_snippet:
Hi all,
I am hoping to use the RJMCMC functionality in nimble to do structure selection across Bayesian networks (DAGs),  where the RJMCMC turns on/off an arc during the sampling. My current thinking

messages.subject: Re: cycle detection - RJMCMC
messages.body_plain:
Hi Fraser,

Thanks for the question.  This looks interesting.

The graph is always static.  It does not dynamically re-determine dependencies (edges) based on node values such as 0.  As a result, you won't be able to write the model as you are, because there is no way around that nimble will throw an error due to the graph being cyclic.

Here are a couple of design ideas.  One is that you could write some mix of user-defined functions and distributions to encompass all of the potentially cyclic nodes.  For example, you could write a user-defined distribution to be used in model code like this:
r[1:n, 1:2] ~ dCustomStuff(beta[1:n, 1:2], flag[1:n])
Inside of dCustomStuff, you could calculate what you need and return -Inf (log of probability=0) if the flags are invalid (if they create a cycle).  You may then want or need to explore customizing how the sampling is done.  This is the route we have taken for example with conditional autoregressive (CAR) models: encapsulate a cyclic sub-graph as a multivariate distribution and provide customized sampling capabilities.

Another idea would be that you could write the model without all the "correct" pieces and then write new samplers that include some of the intended model logic.  For example, you could write

logit(p1[i]) <- beta11

to avoid the cycle but then inside of any sampler for beta11, flag1, or r2[i], you could directly set p1[i] in the sampler's code to what you want, rather than using model$calculate.  And then you could ensure subsequent model calculations are what you need.  The User Manual provides information on writing samplers, and you can use ours as prototypes.  I think this is a more error-prone route because it works around the graph and you would need to ensure that all samplers work correctly (and modify them when you really want to change the model), but I mention it to highlight that in principle you can use the model as a caching device even if you are going to work around graph structure.

HTH!

-Perry

> Hi all,
> I am hoping to use the RJMCMC functionality in nimble to do structure selection across Bayesian networks (DAGs),  where the RJMCMC turns on/off an arc during the sampling. Not sure if this is possible or makes sense but before this I've hit an error with the below toy example  (code below) - nimble throws an error about a detecting a cycle even although both flag1 and flag2 are zero. messages.subject: Constraints in spatial models
messages.body_plain:
Hi to all,
I'm trying to implement a model with lcar prior distribution for spatial random effects. To solve the identifiability problem I want to add the following constraint in my model: sum(ler[1:N])=0.
In the code below you can see how I have implemented the contraints (similar idea as in winbugs) but it doesn't fulfill sum(ler[1:N])=0 condition. I would appreciate any idea/suggestion.
Thanks in advance!
Arantxa

for(i in 1:N) {
    gamma[i] <- expected[i] * exp(alpha0+ler[i])
    RR[i] <- exp(alpha0+ler[i])
    y[i] ~ dpois(gamma[i])

    # Constraints
    cond ~ dnorm(sum.ler, 1000)
    sum.ler <- sum(ler[1:N])
    constraint_data ~ dconstraint(cond = 0)
  }

data <- list(y = y, constraint_data = 1)

messages.subject: Re: cycle detection - RJMCMC
messages.body_plain:
On a little more thought, from your initial code, I think you could use a "dCustomStuff" for each i, something like this:

for(i in 1:n)
r[i, 1:2] ~ dCustomStuff(beta[i, 1:2], flag[i, 1:2])

I am not clear if you intend a one-to-one relationship between indicators (flags) and coefficients.  (Your code has a beta22 but not a beta12).  If so, I think the RJMCMC as written would work.  I think you would first need to modify the default samplers returned by configureMCMC (using $removeSamplers and $addSampler) so that each r[i, j] has a scalar sampler.  If not, I think you would need to build upon our RJMCMC code, e.g. if you want one indicator to be used for multiple coefficients.

-Perry

Hi Perry,
the goal is structure learning in BNs - this is a classic example
https://arxiv.org/ftp/arxiv/papers/1206/1206.5247.pdf - which uses
MCMC to sample across the landscape of DAGs, but this only works for
networks which have the marginal likelihood available in closed form
(so multivariate normal or multinomial). Using RJMCMC it should in
theory be possible to allow more general BN models to be sampled
across as this avoids the difficult marginal likelihood computation.
At least that's my thinking. A 1 to 1 flag to coefficient is all I
need. I'm new to nimble so I'd need to read up on how to do define
r[i,1:2] as a joint density but then have each r[i,j] as a scalar
sampler but this sounds just what I need :-) Thanks, I'll try and
sketch out some code! Fraser.

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I built a model and I plan to run it using PMCMC. It took about an hour to finish running the "buildMCMC()" step and often when I run the sampler, I encounter errors (e.g., logProb of data node y[x,x] is -Inf). I wish to test if changing my data (y) or initial values of the parameters would make the problem go away. Currently, I had to change the data/init from the model object, reconfigure the MCMC and redo the "buildMCMC" to achieve that. This means I need to spend an hour every time I make changes to the data/init.

Is there a simpler and faster way to do that without having to redo "buildMCMC"?

Thank you!

Ben

> >>>>

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thank you for your previous suggestions. For the time being, I have been running cross-validation over the nodes containing data only (i.e. the first 5 [out of 6 total] replicate surveys during each season). This at least gives results. Do you also have an update on what the Development Team suggests for running cross-validation on models with datasets containing NAs in the dependent variable(s)?

On a different note, for a dynamic N-occupancy model (i.e. including sub-models for occupancy and abundance and associated measurement errors for y_occ ~ dbern(psi) and y_abund ~ dbin(N, p) input dependent data), is runCrossValidate( ) able to generate performance scores from a loss function on two processes, both occupancy and abundance? Specifically, this would yield an RMSE for the occupancy process as well as one for the abundance process.

To do so, I have been experimenting with the following code:
#Cross-validate model results
commNocc_FoldFunction <- function(i){
  foldNodes_i <- c(paste0('Yc_abund[', i,', , , ]'), paste0('Yc_occ[', i,', , , ]'))  # will return 'y[1,,,]' for i = 1 (e.g., based on nsite)
  ##foldNodes_i <- c(paste0('Yc_occ[', i,', , , ]'), paste0('Yc_abund[', i,', , , ]'))  # changing the order because the measurement error process for Yc_abund appears first in modelCode
  return(foldNodes_i)
}

# The function below computes the root mean squared error

RMSE_lossFunction <- function(simulatedDataValues, actualDataValues){
  dataLength <- length(simulatedDataValues) # simulatedDataValues is a vector
  SSE <- 0
  for(i in 1:dataLength){
    SSE <- SSE + (simulatedDataValues[i] - actualDataValues[i])^2
  }
  MSE <- SSE / dataLength
  RMSE <- sqrt(MSE)
  return(RMSE)
}

######### Here is where I exclude the 6th replicate surveys#########
win.data$Yc_abund <- win.data$Yc_abund[,,,1:5]
win.data$Yc_occ <- win.data$Yc_occ[,,,1:5]
const$nrep <- dim(win.data$Yc_abund)[[4]]
#####################################################

model <- nimbleModel(code = modelCode, name = "modelCode",
                     constants = const, data = win.data,
                     inits = init)
Cmodel <- compileNimble(model)
modelConf <- configureMCMC(model)

cvSamples <- runCrossValidate(MCMCconfiguration = modelConf,
                               k = 5, foldFunction = commNocc_FoldFunction,
                               lossFunction = RMSE_lossFunction,
                               MCMCcontrol = list(niter = ni, nburnin = nb))

I have also received some puzzling errors from runCrossValidate( ), errors suggesting missing quotations, parentheses, or curly braces, such as:
Error: unexpected '}' in:
"  SSE <-
  }"

or

Error: object 'SSE' not found

or

Error: unexpected '}' in:

"  dataLength <- length(simulatedDataValues) # simulatedDataValues is a vector

  SSE <-  }"

or

Error: unexpected end of input

###

Do these error messages indicate that runCrossValidate( ) cannot handle models with more than one dependent variable, or is my syntax for the foldFunction incorrect?

messages.subject: Re: Changing data or initial values after "buildMCMC()"?
messages.subject_clean: Changing data or initial values after "buildMCMC()"?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, you can simply change the values in the model, without rebuilding the MCMC.  You don't need to rebuild the model object, nor rebuild the MCMC, nor compile these.  You can just use the same (compiled) model and MCMC objects that you're using.  To change values in the (compiled) model, you have many options:

model$x <- 3
model$y <- c(1, 2, 3)

or:
model$setInits( list(x = 1, y = c(1, 2,3) )

or, this also sets values in the model, but also changes which are considered data:
model$setData( list(x = 1, y = c(1, 2,3) )

Then, re-run the MCMC, and it will use those new initial values in the model.

I hope this helps,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Constraints in spatial models
messages.body_plain:
Yes, Arantxa, assuming that the ler[1:N] is the vector of spatial random effects, and that you're using the improper (icar) distribution for these effect (which is the dcar_normal distribution in NIMBLE), then you might just want the zero-mean constraint for these, which is an option with the dcar_normal distribution, which is used as:

ler[1:N] ~ dcar_normal(..., zero_mean = 1)

You can read more about this option, and the dcar_normal distribution in general, by getting the help on the distribution as:

library(nimble)
help(dcar_normal)

As for manually implementing this zero-sum constraint, as you were were doing, I think what you'd want is almost the same as you had, but rather:

code <- modelCode({

    sum.ler <- sum(ler[1:N])

    one ~ constraint(sum.ler = 0)
})

data <- list(..., one = 1)

This approach, using dconstraint to impose the sum-to-zero, could also be used with other distributions for the random effects, for example the dcar_proper distribution.

Hope this gets it working for you!  Let us know if you have other questions.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Monitor only a single (or subset) of entries in vector/matrix
messages.subject_clean: Monitor only a single (or subset) of entries in vector/matrix
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I have a large dataset in a regression type model and I would like to generate realizations of the posterior predictive distribution for the response variables given certain covariate patterns of predictors. I can do this but not without monitoring the entire dataset which is resulting in massive (redundant) output files. For example I want to monitor y[39300,1:3] (which are set to NAs in the dataset) and don't want all y[1:39299,1:3] as these are all fixed data values.  I've put the full code listing below.

Any suggestions greatly appreciated!
thanks.
Fraser

### code listing end to end
rm(list=ls())
gc();
load("isaac_m.RData");# provides isaac.m - a BIG matrix

# create empty response (for one covariate pattern) to get predictive distn.
extraNA1<-isaac.m[1,] # grab first row and set responses to NAs
extraNA1[1:3]<-NA
isaac.m<-rbind(isaac.m,extraNA1) # append to end of data

library(parallel)

this_cluster <- makeCluster(20)

set.seed(10120)
#seeds=1;

run_MCMC_allcode <- function(seeds,dat) {

  library(nimble, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

  code <- nimbleCode({

    sigma ~ dunif(0, 20)  ## uniform prior per Gelman (2006)
    psi ~ dunif(0,1)    ## prior on inclusion probability

    for(j in 1:r){
      beta0[j] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma)
    }

    z21 ~ dbern(psi) ## indicator variable for each coefficient
    beta21 ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma)
    z21beta21 <- z21 * beta21
    z31 ~ dbern(psi)
    beta31 ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma)
    z31beta31 <- z31 * beta31
    z32 ~ dbern(psi)
    beta32 ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma)
    z32beta32 <- z32 * beta32

    for(k in 1:c){
      z1[k] ~ dbern(psi)
      beta1[k] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma)
      z1beta1[k] <- z1[k]*beta1[k]

      z2[k] ~ dbern(psi)
      beta2[k] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma)
      z2beta2[k] <- z2[k]*beta2[k]

      z3[k] ~ dbern(psi)
      beta3[k] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sigma)
      z3beta3[k] <- z3[k]*beta3[k]
    }

    for(i in 1:n) {

    # DAG structure for response - 3-dim logistic output
    # Y1 curEczema_EC03x -> Y2 curRhinitis_RH02 -> Y3 curAsthma_WH02
    #  curEczema_EC03x  ---  curRhinitis_RH02
    #  curEczema_EC03x  ---  curAsthma_WH02
    #  curRhinitis_RH02  ---  curAsthma_WH02
    # can't resolve to use
    # curEczema_EC03x  ->  curRhinitis_RH02 -> curAsthma_WH02
    # curEczema_EC03x  ----------------------> curAsthma_WH02

     logit(p1[i]) <- beta0[1] + inprod(z1beta1[1:c], x1[i, 1:c]) # Eczema
     y[i,1] ~ dbern(p1[i])

     logit(p2[i]) <- beta0[2] + inprod(z2beta2[1:c], x1[i, 1:c]) + z21beta21*y[i,1] # Rhinitis
     y[i,2] ~ dbern(p2[i])

     logit(p3[i]) <- beta0[3] + inprod(z3beta3[1:c], x1[i, 1:c]) + z31beta31*y[i,1] + z32beta32*y[i,2] # Asthma
     y[i,3] ~ dbern(p3[i])

     }
   })

  isaac.m=dat[[1]];

constants <- list(n = nrow(isaac.m), c=13, r=3, x1 = isaac.m[,c("RF09_01",
                                                                        "RF09_02",
                                                                        "RF09_03",
                                                                        "RF09_01x",
                                                                        "RF10_01",
                                                                        "RF10_02",
                                                                        "RF10_03",
                                                                        "RF10_01x",
                                                                        "RF09101x",
                                                                        "RF09102x",
                                                                        "RF09103x",
                                                                        "RF09104x",
                                                                        "DC01" )])

data <- list(y = isaac.m[,c("curEczema_EC03x","curRhinitis_RH02","curAsthma_WH02")])

inits <- list(beta0 = rep(0.1,3), beta1 = rep(0.1,13),beta2 = rep(0.4,13),beta3 = rep(0.5,13), beta21=0.1,beta31=0.2, beta32=0.2,
              z21=0,z31=0,z32=0,z1=rep(0,13),z2=rep(0,13),z3=rep(0,13),
              sigma=1,psi=0.1)

model <- nimbleModel(code, constants = constants, data = data, inits = inits) # build model

mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(model,print=TRUE) # assign default samplers to nodes
mcmcConf$addMonitors('y[39300,1]','beta0','beta1','beta2','beta3','beta21','beta31','beta32','z21','z31','z32','z1','z2','z3',
                     'z21beta21','z31beta31','z32beta32','z1beta1','z2beta2','z3beta3','sigma','psi')

configureRJ(mcmcConf,
            targetNodes = c('beta1','beta2','beta3','beta21','beta31','beta32'),
            indicatorNodes = c('z1','z2','z3','z21','z31','z32'),
            control = list(mean = 0, scale = .2))

mcmcConf$printSamplers(c("z3[6]", "beta3[6]"))

myMCMC <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)

Cmodel <- compileNimble(model,resetFunctions = TRUE)
CmodelMCMC <- compileNimble(myMCMC, project = Cmodel,resetFunctions = TRUE)

results <- runMCMC(CmodelMCMC, niter = 200000,thin=20,nchains=1,setSeed=seeds,
                   samplesAsCodaMCMC = FALSE)

return(results);
}

chain_output <- parLapply(cl = this_cluster, X = 1:20, ## NOTE this is the seeds argument!
                          fun = run_MCMC_allcode,
                          dat=list(isaac.m) # this is one extra argument
                          )

# It's good practice to close the cluster when you're done with it.
stopCluster(this_cluster)

hi Andrew,

Regarding handling of NAs, I'd need more information on what your goal is in order to be able to respond usefully. Given one can't use an NA to calculate a loss, it's not clear to me what it means to include values with NAs in a held-out set. Do you just want nimble to be able to handle this for convenience - i.e., that nodes with NAs could be included in a fold but would be ignored? If so, that's something we could probably do quite easily, though the development team would have to discuss if it's something we want as part of the user interface.

Regarding your syntax errors, those indeed look odd. Would you be able to share a minimal reproducible example (off-list if you prefer) so I can look in more detail?

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Fraser,

A couple thoughts here:

1) Rewrite the names in the model such that y[39300,1:3] is not part of 'y', but has its own variable name.

2) Don't include y in the monitors. Instead sample from the posterior predictive after the MCMC is done, using R code that makes use of the model and the MCMC output or writing a nimbleFunction that makes use of the model and the MCMC output. This would require monitoring any nodes that are directly involved in the posterior predictive distribution(s) of interest.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
I was just sketching out the second idea Chris shared:

One option is you could do what you want with a separate nimbleFunction.  Something like this (untested) seems like what you are describing:

predictorNF <- nimbleFunction(
  setup = function(model, input_nodes, output_nodes) {
     update_nodes <- model$getDependencies(input_nodes)
     length_output_nodes <- length(model$expandNodeNames(output_nodes, returnScalarComponents=TRUE))
  },
  run = function(MCMCmatrix = double(2)) {
    m <- dim(MCMCmatrix)[1] # number of saved MCMC iterations
    outputMatrix <- matrix(nrow = m, ncol = length_output_nodes)
    for(i in 1:m) {
       values(model, input_nodes) <<- MCMCmatrix[i,] # You'll need to be sure the order of input_nodes matches the column order of MCMCmatrix
       model$calculate(update_nodes) # update anything that depends on input_nodes
       model$simulate(output_nodes) # insert "includeData = TRUE" if you need to simulate new values into data nodes
       outputMatrix[i, ] <- values(model, output_nodes)
       return(outputMatrix)
       returnType(double(2))
    }
  }

# input_nodes is a vector of node names of the parameters you want to change for simulations.  E.g these would be a subset of column names in the MCMC output.
# output_nodes is a vector of node names of posterior predictive nodes you want to simulate for each row of the input.
myPredictorNF <- predictorNF(model, input_nodes, output_nodes)
# please run uncompiled for debugging
myPredictorNF$run(MCMCsamples)
# then compile
CmyPredictorNF <- compileNimble(myPredictorNF, project = model)

Again, this is untested.  I'm hoping it conveys the idea of what you'd want to do.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for the feedback.

Regarding the NAs, yeah, it's mostly about adding user convenience to runCrossValidate( ), especially in light of observational studies. You're absolutely right that loss cannot be computed from non-data; that certainly wasn't my ask, and I apologize if my previous messages were somewhat unclear.

Following your suggestions from a couple of weeks ago, I attempted to code fold functions that would "ignore" or "skip over" NAs in the dependent variables, but each of those attempts were unsuccessful, which is likely due to my lack of complete understanding of NIMBLE's under-the-hood operations for runCrossValidate( ). For example, it wasn't clear to me how I could exclude NAs in either my fold function or in the simulatedDataValues or actualDataValues within my loss function. Instead, I decided to take a simpler approach and just leave out the NAs entirely by removing the 6th replicates in both seasons a priori, limiting model validation to an extent. Recall that NAs only occurred in my dependent variables during (missing) 6th replicate surveys in the first season.

About the syntax errors, I really don't know what went wrong, but it's no longer a problem after a re-run. I didn't make any changes to the input code (e.g., because I did not see any comma, parenthesis, or bracket problems), and no errors were ultimately thrown. I have no idea what occurred the first time. If you'd still like to see a reproducible, then I would be happy to forward you one off-list.

Best,
Andrew

messages.subject: Re: Constraints in spatial models
messages.body_plain:
Arantxa, thanks again for following up.  It looks like you're running into a nuanced case of the dconstraint distribution, and making that work for you would be another discussion.

But more importantly, after sending my email yesterday, I realized that using the dconstraint distribution to impose the sum-to-zero will lead to other, bigger, problems, with the spatial CAR process.  Basically, if we correctly were to use the dconstraint distribution to impose this, then during the course of MCMC sampling, none of the spatial components (the elements of ler[]) would be able to transition (since no proposed transition to a single element of lew[] would satisfy this constraint), and essentially the MCMC would fail to correctly sample.  This approach wouldn't work.

Instead, the best mechanism I think would be making use of the zero_mean argument, as we also discussed.  This will impose a zero mean, and hence also sum-to-zero, for the spatial components, but also will allow correct MCMC sampling.  Is that what you're after?

Daniel

On Wed, Dec 30, 2020 at 12:32 PM Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu> wrote:
> Yes, Arantxa, assuming that the ler[1:N] is the vector of spatial random effects, and that you're using the improper (icar) distribution for these effect (which is the dcar_normal distribution in NIMBLE), then you might just want the zero-mean constraint for these, which is an option with the dcar_normal distribution, which is used as:
>
> ler[1:N] ~ dcar_normal(..., zero_mean = 1)
>
> You can read more about this option, and the dcar_normal distribution in general, by getting the help on the distribution as:
>
> library(nimble)
> help(dcar_normal)
>
> As for manually implementing this zero-sum constraint, as you were were doing, I think what you'd want is almost the same as you had, but rather:
>
> code <- modelCode({
>     sum.ler <- sum(ler[1:N])
>     one ~ constraint(sum.ler = 0)
> })
>
> data <- list(..., one = 1)
>
> This approach, using dconstraint to impose the sum-to-zero, could also be used with other distributions for the random effects, for example the dcar_proper distribution.
>
> Hope this gets it working for you!  Let us know if you have other questions.
>
> Cheers,
> Daniel
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Fraser, it looks like you're already on the right track.  I'll just re-mention, that Chris's first suggestion ("Rewrite the names in the model such that y[39300,1:3] is not part of 'y', but has its own variable name") is a really dead-simple and easy way to go.  Implementing that strategy would look like:

code <- nimbleCode({
    .....
    yPred[1:3] <- y[39300,1:3]    ## add this line to your model code
})

Then, when you add MCMC monitors (mcmcConf$addMonitors), don't add any monitors to any parts of "y", and instead:

mcmcConf$addMonitors(..., "yPred")

That's all you'd need to do.  This approach has the added cost of adding 3 more nodes (actually only 1 node, a length-3 vector) to your model, which is not a large overhead when compared to everything else going on.  And it has the advantage of simplicity.

Cheers,
Daniel

And, finally, there is the option of using monitors2 with its own thinning interval, thin2, to record some states less frequently (in iterations) than others.

> Fraser, it looks like you're already on the right track.  I'll just re-mention, that Chris's first suggestion ("Rewrite the names in the model such that y[39300,1:3] is not part of 'y', but has its own variable name") is a really dead-simple and easy way to go.  Implementing that strategy would look like:
>
> code <- nimbleCode({
>     .....
>     yPred[1:3] <- y[39300,1:3]    ## add this line to your model code
> })
>
> Then, when you add MCMC monitors (mcmcConf$addMonitors), don't add any monitors to any parts of "y", and instead:
>
> mcmcConf$addMonitors(..., "yPred")
>
> That's all you'd need to do.  This approach has the added cost of adding 3 more nodes (actually only 1 node, a length-3 vector) to your model, which is not a large overhead when compared to everything else going on.  And it has the advantage of simplicity.
>
> Cheers,
> Daniel
>
>
>

> > > predictorNF <- nimbleFunction(

> > >      update_nodes <- model$getDependencies(input_nodes)
> > >      length_output_nodes <- length(model$expandNodeNames(output_nodes, returnScalarComponents=TRUE))
> > >   },
> > >   run = function(MCMCmatrix = double(2)) {
> > >     m <- dim(MCMCmatrix)[1] # number of saved MCMC iterations
> > >     outputMatrix <- matrix(nrow = m, ncol = length_output_nodes)
> > >     for(i in 1:m) {
> > >        values(model, input_nodes) <<- MCMCmatrix[i,] # You'll need to be sure the order of input_nodes matches the column order of MCMCmatrix
> > >        model$calculate(update_nodes) # update anything that depends on input_nodes
> > >        model$simulate(output_nodes) # insert "includeData = TRUE" if you need to simulate new values into data nodes
> > >        outputMatrix[i, ] <- values(model, output_nodes)
> > >        return(outputMatrix)
> > >        returnType(double(2))
> > >     }
> > >   }

> > > # input_nodes is a vector of node names of the parameters you want to change for simulations.  E.g these would be a subset of column names in the MCMC output.

> > > # please run uncompiled for debugging

> > > # then compile
